teaser: Users can now rebuild the part of a product they need; what stops them is maintenance. Vendors should sell that, as villagers and town planners.
core_idea: When users can rebuild the 10% of a product they need, every friction becomes a decision, and what stops them is maintaining what they built; a software company should position itself, in Wardley's terms, as the villager and town planner under its users, letting them explore on top of the product by talking to it and selling them the maintenance of their versions, from a pound to a maintained fork; Firefox, a good browser funded about 73% by royalties from mostly one customer, is the example of a product that could take that money instead.

figures.caption: A product as explorers, villagers and town planners: users explore on top, talking to the app, keeping a personal version and writing the best brief the vendor will get; the vendor maintains customisations and turns popular ones into features; the core is a set of primitives, deterministic and accountable.

Four ways a user would pay the vendor: explore, free or a pound a month; keep, ten to fifty pounds a year for changes maintained across releases; adopt, fifty to five hundred pounds a change built properly; own, a maintained fork by contract.
